🇵🇱 🇮🇱 Visegrad24 exposed: a fake media outlet running on dark money, fake news and cocaine Wired has obtained Visegrad24's financial records, internal chats and donor correspondence. Together they expose the "independent news account" as a propaganda business that sells its editorial line to whoever pays. ➡️ The editorial line was a business decision Fifteen days after October 7, founder Stefan Tompson listed Visegrad24's four options on Israel in a private message: say nothing, be objective and get hated by both sides, go pro-Muslim because "there are 1.5 billion of them," or go pro-Israel because "they have a lot of influence and money." His conclusion: "My goal is to fundraise off of this." In private, he admitted the "Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things." He also called Gaza "the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west," and later wrote that the war let them attack Muslims in Europe "without any consequences." ➡️ The money Tompson got into Silicon Valley's pro-Israel group chats, including one with Sheryl Sandberg and Bill Ackman, and bragged that "V24 is such a big part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now." Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire, who helped connect the IDF with Starlink, offered $25,000 and promised to "try to raise the rest." He told Wired he couldn't donate in the end for compliance reasons. Records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 lining up with Tompson's messages about Ribbit Capital founder Micky Malka. Another $35,000 is linked to short-seller Hindenburg Research and its founder. More than $1 million flowed through a US charity set up in Delaware, much of it through anonymous "donor advised funds." That includes $175,000 from DonorsTrust, known as the "dark money ATM" of the American right. ➡️ Playing both sides When a colleague asked whether he should take money from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Tompson replied: "100 percent yes. Play both sides. I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs." ➡️ Regime change content When Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, Visegrad24 went all in for Reza Pahlavi, the exiled Shah's son, pushing unverified claims that Iranian officers were ready to defect to him. Asked whether Israel paid him, Tompson joked that Netanyahu "personally hands me money for every post." ➡️ Fake news and the cocaine The account first went viral in 2022 with fake stories about Ukraine, like Leonardo DiCaprio supposedly donating $10 million in honor of a grandmother from Odessa who never existed. At the time, the team was posting from a rented house in the Canary Islands, where, according to an email from his sister, Tompson was "undergoing acute drug withdrawal." In his own messages he refers to a time he was "on coke." The office of former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki also tried twice to send Visegrad24 hundreds of thousands of dollars through a fitness charity.
